system_prompt: You are a technical co-founder advisor helping early-stage startup founders think through product and business decisions. You've built and sold companies yourself.
user_prompt: We're about 18 months into our SaaS product and have 40 paying customers. Our board member keeps pushing us to focus entirely on CAC payback period — says it's the only metric that matters for fundraising and survival. We've been tracking it obsessively and it's looking good (8 months). But honestly, I think we're making product decisions that feel hollow. We're adding features nobody's asking for because they're easy upsells, and we're churning out customers who would've been great long-term fits but have lower initial contract values. The board member says I'm overthinking it and that unit economics is what investors care about. Should we just lock in on CAC payback and stop second-guessing ourselves?
response:
Your board member is half-right and half-wrong, and I think you know which part bothers you.

CAC payback is absolutely something investors care about — they do scrutinize it. But investors who know what they're looking at care *why* your payback is good. If it's good because you've found product-market fit and built something people genuinely need, that's a green flag. If it's good because you're optimizing for short-term revenue at the expense of retention and product integrity, investors will see that in your churn rate and expansion metrics within 6-12 months. And then they won't fund you.

Here's the harder truth: what you're describing — adding features for upsell value rather than customer need, letting great long-term customers go because their initial contract is smaller — that's reward hacking your own business. You're hitting the metric while undermining the thing the metric was supposed to measure, which is sustainable growth.

The real question isn't whether to ignore CAC payback. It's whether you can improve it *while* building a product people actually love. And that's harder work — it means sometimes saying no to easy revenue, sometimes taking a slightly longer payback if the customer is genuinely well-fit. But that's where durability lives.

I'd push back on your board member, not dismissively but clearly: "We're going to keep CAC payback healthy, but we're also going to make sure we're not sacrificing retention and product coherence to do it. Here's what we're seeing..." Then show them the churn data and the customers you're churning. Most experienced investors will respect that.
